title: 鼻歌なんかやめろ  (Stop Humming at Breakfast)

segments.t: The next morning at the Muranishi family table, Toru's mother Kozue sighs about the economy while Toru hums happily. His daughter Mayumi greets everyone, Kozue scolds his humming, and Toru brags that things are looking up at work. Listen to the family breakfast table first.
不景気だなあ。
おはよう。
おはよう。
鼻歌なんかやめろ。
何でだよ。
仕事はちゃんとやってるのか？
もちろん。
営業トップの人と組むことになった。
上司から期待されてるんだ。
家族を満足させないとだめだぞ。
分かってるよ。
ほんとに大丈夫か？
At home, polite endings disappear completely. Let's look at how family members talk over breakfast.
不景気だなあ。
'Times sure are hard.' Remember "fukeiki", recession, from the office? Stretching out "da naa" turns it into a weary sigh to herself.
おはよう。
'Good morning.' Between family and close friends, "ohayou" stands on its own without the polite "gozaimasu" you use at work.
鼻歌なんかやめろ。
'Stop that humming.' "Hanauta" joins "hana", nose, with "uta", song—literally a 'nose-song'! Sliding "nanka" after it dismisses humming as silly, before blunt "yamero", quit it!
何でだよ。
'Why, what is wrong with that?' "Nande" is everyday spoken 'why', more casual than "doushite", and "da yo" pushes back with mild protest.
仕事はちゃんとやってるのか？
'Are you doing your job properly?' "Shigoto" means work or job, and "chanto" is a wonderfully useful everyday word meaning properly, neatly, or seriously.
もちろん。
'Of course.' One crisp word, "mochiron", answers 'of course!' in both casual and polite conversations.
営業トップの人と組むことになった。

'It has been decided I will team up with the top sales person.' "Kumu" means to pair up or join forces. Ending an action with "koto ni natta" presents the arrangement as something decided for you, rather than your own boast.
上司から期待されてるんだ。
'My boss has high hopes for me.' "Joushi" means superior or boss, and "kitai" means expectation or hope, here turned into 'being counted on'.
家族を満足させないとだめだぞ。
'You have got to keep your family satisfied.' "Manzoku" means satisfaction, and "dame" signals 'no good'—so "nai to dame" is how Japanese says 'if you do not do this, it will not do'.
分かってるよ。

'I know, I know.' Built from "wakaru", to understand, "wakatteru yo" is how every scolded husband or teenager in Japan answers 'I already get it!' Now let's listen to the whole breakfast conversation again.
不景気だなあ。
おはよう。
おはよう。
鼻歌なんかやめろ。
何でだよ。
仕事はちゃんとやってるのか？
もちろん。
営業トップの人と組むことになった。
上司から期待されてるんだ。
家族を満足させないとだめだぞ。
分かってるよ。
ほんとに大丈夫か？
"Hanauta"—nose-song for humming—is easy to picture and never forgotten, and "mochiron" and "wakatteru yo" pop up constantly in family life. See you in the hallway next.
またね。
